Designing for the quietest residents of the Indian household.

mitraa is a mobile platform that helps Indian adults over 55 discover, join and host local social events — guided by Miro, an AI companion built for people who know what they want to do but not how to start.

Shruti’s Role
Sole designer & researcher
Timeline
Jul’ 2025 – Mar’ 2026
Context
M.Des Thesis, IIT Hyderabad
Discipline
UX Research · Product Design

01 — Overview

Loneliness is not an absence of people. It is an absence of purpose.

India will be home to roughly 319 million people aged 60 and above by 2050 — every fifth Indian a senior citizen. The national conversation about that shift is almost entirely about health and money. This thesis argues the harder, more neglected problem is the emotional and social architecture of later life.

The research began where most Indian design research does — in a specific, ordinary memory. An elderly couple lived next door to my family in Patna. The husband was paralysed, the wife semi-bedridden. Their children, in another city, paid for a nurse twice a day and a house-help for meals. When either was unavailable, food arrived at the door and stayed there, because neither of them could collect it.

Their children would call my mother. She would go over, help them eat, and stay a little longer to talk. Their home was usually latched from the outside. Both have since passed away. What stayed with me was not the physical dependence — it was how thoroughly the emotional dependence went unnamed by everyone involved.

FOCUS 01

Companionship

Recurring social touchpoints that reduce isolation — built as rituals, not programmes.

FOCUS 02

Contentedness

Space to express skill and hold an identity beyond the caregiver or retiree role.

FOCUS 03

Community

Structured activity that becomes part of a daily routine rather than an optional addition to it.

mitraa — from mitra, friend. Scope deliberately excludes medical intervention, geriatric care and disability management; it addresses emotional wellness, engagement and cultural empowerment within the existing capacities of its users.

02 — Problem statement

Elders who are financially comfortable and physically capable still report being no longer useful.

A pattern surfaced across every conversation, survey response and observation: elderly individuals are not lonely because they lack people. They are lonely because they lack purpose, participation and a sense of being needed.

With urban migration accelerating and nuclear families becoming the norm, the support structures that once kept elders embedded in social life have fractured. Elders who were the axis around which a household turned have gradually become its quietest residents. They perform happiness because it is easier than explaining the alternative.

The loss of a daily role, the shrinking of peer circles, the slow disappearance of the routines that gave a day its shape — these are not medical problems. They are design problems. The opportunity is not in healthcare or welfare. It is in belonging, purpose and structured social engagement.

They say sab theek hai. Everything is fine. Thesis — Problem definition

03 — Research & insights

Six methods, one recurring answer.

Primary research combined an interview with a geriatric psychiatrist, an interview with an elderly shelter-home administrator, conversational surveys with elderly residents in Bengaluru, ethnographic observation in community parks, and structured surveys with young adults living away from their parents — triangulated against government and NGO desk research.

47young adults living away from their parents, surveyed
40+senior citizens of 2 distinct elder community clubs have participated in activity based public survey
21elder shelter home residents were observed and their care taker has been surveyed
1geriatric psychiatrist was interviewed

A gendered split in access to social space

Observation at a Bengaluru park revealed a sharp contrast. Elderly men had morning yoga groups and evening carrom circles — social connection, mental stimulation, a channel for stories, a buffer against loneliness.

Elderly women largely did not. Their engagement stayed indoors, restricted to a spouse or phone calls, with identity still tied to care roles and rituals. This gap is a recurring theme in Indian gerontology literature, and it directly shaped two product decisions: the women-only filter and skill badges.

Retirement often triggers a sharp decline in mental stimulation. Dr. Meena Medikonda, geriatric psychiatrist

Her core finding: emotional isolation emerges not from physical solitude but from reduced responsibility, lack of routine and diminished purpose. Elders hesitate to express needs because they do not want to burden their children.

Many residents long for a familiar face at the gate, but the gate stays mostly empty. Alex Paul, shelter home administrator

Between 60 and 80% of his residents need daily assistance. Most families pay the fees but rarely visit. Micro-engagement activities like candle-making brought real joy, and were discontinued for want of staff.

03b — The numbers

What the desk research established.

Living arrangements of Indian elders

The joint family has not vanished — but a third of elders now live without a spouse present, or entirely alone.

  • With spouse and children62%
  • With children, without spouse26%
  • With spouse only7%
  • Living alone5%

Source: HelpAge India, Ageing in India: Exploring Preparedness & Response to Care Challenges (2022).

The gaps the system leaves open

Financial, clinical and digital exclusion compound each other — and none of them are what elders named first.

Lack any pension coverage78%
Report limitations in activities of daily living24%
Experience mental health issues20%
Have any health insurance18%
Aged 60+ who have ever used the internet13%

Sources: NITI Aayog senior care reforms report (2022); Longitudinal Ageing Study of India. General-population internet use is roughly 50%.

Depression among Indian elders is roughly ten times more common than diagnosis records suggest.

Depressive symptoms are present in nearly a third of the elderly population. The prevalence of probable depression is close to ten times higher than self-reported diagnoses — the condition is widespread and largely unnamed.

Source: Longitudinal Ageing Study of India, via NITI Aayog (2022).

~⅓ of older adults show depressive symptoms

04 — Personas

Three profiles, built from field data rather than assumption.

Each persona represents a distinct profile within the 55+ audience, drawn from observation, survey responses and interview material. Each one also exposes a different gap in the product.

Persona 01

Jitendra Shahi

64 · Bengaluru · Retired banker · Widower, lives alone

“I’m not one for apps — but my daughter trusts it.”
Core need
Peer friendship and structured routine outside the family
Barrier
Low tech confidence; reluctant to try anything unfamiliar alone
Gap it exposed
Attending events is easy. Converting acquaintances into friends is not — hence the post-event friend nudge.

Persona 02

Menka Jain

61 · Bengaluru · Former entrepreneur · Grandchildren’s caregiver

“I feel like just ‘Arjun’s mom’. I want to feel like myself again.”
Core need
Reclaim a creative identity beyond the caregiver role
Barrier
Limited uninterrupted time; fear her expertise won’t be valued
Gap it exposed
Safety and comfort are prerequisites for hosting — the women-only filter and skill badges are not enhancements, they are entry conditions.

Persona 03

Alok & Nitu Patel

69 & 62 · Bengaluru 33 years · Empty nesters

“Our children are settled far away; Bengaluru still needs to feel like home.”
Core need
Build a new local social network together, as a couple
Barrier
The app treats them as two individuals, not one unit
Gap it exposed
No joint profile, no co-host, no couple-friendly tag, no joint RSVP — a blind spot affecting a large share of the 55+ demographic.

Journey sentiment across six stages

Journey maps were built for all three personas across awareness, onboarding, discovery, joining an event, creating an event and ongoing use — tracking actions, thoughts, emotions, pain points, opportunities and Miro touchpoints at each stage.

Jitendra — dips at first attendance, recovers sharply Menka — highest variance, dips at first hosting Alok & Nitu — smooth, consistently rising

Qualitative sentiment curves transcribed from the journey maps in the source deck. These describe the shape of each persona’s emotional arc as documented in research — they are not measured quantitative data.

Six opportunities from cross-referencing the journey maps

01

Attendee preview before joining

All three personas need to know who will be there before committing. A visible attendee count and age-range preview measurably reduces social anxiety.

02

Couple profile & joint RSVP

A linked profile and joint-join feature would serve the large share of 55+ users who experience social life as a unit rather than as individuals.

03

Women-only filter & skill badges

Safety filters and expertise visibility determine whether this segment uses the platform at all. Not optional enhancements.

04

Post-event friend nudge

A one-tap connection prompt immediately after an event closes the gap between shared activity and actual friendship.

05

Save & resume onboarding

Menka is interrupted by childcare; Jitendra tires quickly. Short-session support reduces drop-off at the most critical acquisition moment.

06

Recurring event templates

All three personas settle into routines. Recurring events remove the friction of sustained hosting and reinforce daily structure.

05 — Process, IA & user flow

Two biases had to be removed before the concept worked.

Technology-first bias

Early concepts defaulted to elaborate digital features, forgetting that the user base includes people who struggle with basic app navigation. Every feature was then stress-tested against one question: can a 65-year-old with basic WhatsApp familiarity use this without help? Anything more than three taps deep, or that assumed digital confidence, was redesigned or removed.

Welfare bias

Several early directions framed elders as recipients of care — people who needed helping. Field research contradicted this flatly. Every participant expressed a desire to contribute, to be useful, to give rather than only receive. The final concept positions elders as hosts, organisers, teachers and cultural contributors, not beneficiaries.

Information architecture

Designed around a single constraint: no screen is more than three taps from the home screen. Four bottom-navigation sections, three persistent header icons, and one shared destination.

Bottom nav Four primary sections
Dashboard — Miro suggestions, memories, preference topics Discover — nearby events, category filters, save, join request Create — AI-assisted and manual paths Plans — joined events, updates feed, withdraw participation
Header Persistent across every screen
Friends — list, nearby people, in-app call, share event Notifications — event updates, friend requests, Miro alerts Profile — personal details, location, preferences, account settings
Shared destination The Event Page
Organiser view — edit, dissolve, invite friends, chat, joinee list Joinee view — details, organiser profile, chat, withdraw, landmark pin Chat room — group chat plus a pinned landmark image and note
Floating layer Miro, the AI companion
Onboarding psych quizDaily event suggestions Voice-to-event pre-fillPlain-language navigation help Post-event friend nudgeMemory highlights

Miro floats over the entire IA — it accelerates navigation rather than replacing it. Users who prefer to browse can ignore it entirely.

Primary flow — first open to first event

1App launch→ 2Sign up→ 3Profile setup→ 4Miro psych quiz→ 5Dashboard→ 6Discover→ 7Event Page→ 8Join request→ 9Chat + landmark pin→ 10Attendance→ 11Post-event friend nudge

Creation flow — voice prompt to published event

1Miro voice or text prompt→ 2Pre-filled form review→ 3Date, time, venue, pricing→ 4Publish→ 5Event Page (organiser)→ 6Invite friends→ 7Chat management

Both flows converge on the Event Page. This was deliberate — the app effectively has one primary destination, and every other section is either a path to it or a management layer around it. Users learn one pattern, not three.

Discover experiences

Calibri · body

Find your next meaningful moment with friends.

Body text and labels, set at a 16pt default — above standard, to accommodate mild vision change.

44pt minimum targets

Minimum touch target size follows accessibility guidance for users above 55, whose precision on small targets is lower than the general population. Usability testing later pushed this to 48pt.

07 — Design solution

Eleven screens, one destination.

High-fidelity screens applying the full system across both the joinee and organiser flows. The Dashboard was designed to feel like a morning notice board rather than a feed — Miro’s suggestions appear as gentle nudges, not algorithmic recommendations.

Hover or focus any screen to pan down its full length.

Login

Phone-first with OTP. No password to remember or reset.

Sign up

Photo is optional. Onboarding collects only what Miro needs to function.

Miro psych quiz

A conversational card format, not a form. Park participants responded to conversation, not questionnaires.

Dashboard

A morning notice board. Memory photos sit at the top, reinforcing belonging and continuity.

Discover

Attendee count is visible without tapping — the single most requested reassurance in research.

Event page

The shared destination. Organiser view surfaces five actions in one scroll; the landmark pin answers “where exactly?”.

Create

Two coexisting paths — Miro pre-fill for newcomers, manual entry for confident users. Same outcome, different effort.

Plans

Withdraw Participation was repositioned and given a confirmation dialog after one tester could not find it.

Friends

In-app calling sits directly in the list. Social context is header-level, never buried in a section.

Profile

Public and private details are visually separated, so users always know what others can see.

Miro, explaining

Navigation questions get answered in plain language — never a redirect to help documentation.

07b — AI intervention

Miro is not a chatbot. It is a shortcut layer.

A persistent, floating guide available on every screen. It removes the barrier between intent and action for a user group that often knows what it wants to do but does not know how to start.

TOUCHPOINT 01

Psychographic onboarding

A conversational quiz mapping interests, activity types, time of day, and comfort with indoor or outdoor settings. The profile persists across the whole journey.

TOUCHPOINT 02

Daily suggestions

Personalised event picks on the Dashboard, refreshed against evolving activity history.

TOUCHPOINT 03

Voice-to-event pre-fill

A spoken or typed description becomes a fully pre-filled event form. Cognitive load drops from a blank form to a review — creation in under 60 seconds.

TOUCHPOINT 04

Plain-language navigation help

Any question about using the app, answered directly via the orange talk button on any screen.

TOUCHPOINT 05

Post-event friend nudge

After an attended event, Miro identifies other attendees worth adding, based on shared interests and proximity.

TOUCHPOINT 06

Memory highlights

Photographs from past events resurface on the Dashboard, reinforcing identity, belonging and continuity over time.

09 — Testing, outcomes & learnings

Three rounds of testing with six participants aged 58 to 70.

Sessions ran in person with the prototype on a tablet. Participants completed tasks unassisted: signing up, finding and joining an event, and creating a new event using Miro. Each round fed directly into the next iteration.

ROUND 01

Highest-severity issues

Found: touch targets below 44pt were missed under normal use. Onboarding took too many screens — two participants abandoned mid-flow. The Miro button went unnoticed by three of six, because orange against the dark header was not immediately legible.

Fixed: all targets raised to 48pt. Onboarding cut to three essential screens with save-and-resume. Miro button given a pulsing ring for the first three sessions.

ROUND 02

Secondary friction

Found: the Event Page organiser view read as cluttered to two participants. The pricing field confused people — was zero required for a free event? One participant could not locate Withdraw Participation.

Fixed: secondary actions moved to an overflow menu. A Free/Paid toggle replaced the raw pricing field. Withdraw Participation repositioned with a confirmation dialog.

ROUND 03

Validation

Found: five of six participants completed every critical task successfully. The sixth needed a single assist during event creation — asking how to set an event to free.

Judgement: noted but not classified as blocking. The toggle was visible; the participant had simply not noticed it.

Verified iterations

Eight changes made and confirmed across the three rounds:

48ptminimum touch target, raised from 44pt
3onboarding screens, down from the original flow
5 / 6participants completed every critical task unassisted
≤ 3taps from home to any screen in the app
  • · Miro button given a pulsing discovery animation for new users
  • · Event Page secondary actions moved to an overflow menu
  • · Free / Paid toggle replaced the raw pricing input
  • · Withdraw Participation repositioned with a confirmation dialog
  • · Landmark pin pinned to the top of chat, separate from the message stream
  • · Women-only filter added to Discover, following feedback from female participants

Impact, at three levels

Individual

Restores daily structure, social routine and a sense of purpose after retirement, widowhood or family migration. Jitendra’s Saturday chess group is not entertainment. It is a reason to wake up with somewhere to be.

Community

The platform makes proximity legible — surfacing that the woman in flat 4B and the retired professor in 9A share an interest in Carnatic music, after six years in the same building.

Family

Reduces the caregiver guilt the surveys identified. Seeing a parent active, hosting and contributing changes the emotional register of distance.

These are not soft outcomes. They are the clinical predictors of better cognitive and physical health in ageing populations. On increased interaction, reduced loneliness and routine stability

Future scope

Features identified during research and testing that fall outside this thesis but represent clear development priorities.

Couple profiles & joint RSVP

Alok and Nitu’s journey map makes the case. A significant share of the 55+ demographic experiences social life as a pair.

Family connect portal

A view for adult children showing their parents’ activity — events attended, connections made, memories. Directly addresses caregiver guilt.

Time banking

Several participants wanted to trade skills for help they need. A credit-based exchange adds an economic dignity layer.

Old age home integration

A version for institutional care with guided programmes and trained facilitators, for an underserved population.

ROOTS integration

The ideation-phase concept connecting elder cultural expertise to GI-tagged product commerce. Where mitraa addresses social engagement, ROOTS addresses economic dignity.

The closing position

India’s demographic shift is already underway. The systems and platforms that serve elderly people have not kept pace. mitraa is one response to that gap. Not a complete solution. A beginning.
